Second, several linked editorials and correspondence were identified in PubMed but not obtained in full, so no critique point on this page is attributed to them: Alipour's editorial on Bardhi 2025 (PMID 40518235), Bridgewater, Webster and Amin's comment on the DRAINAGE trial (PMID 30122357), the four ABC-06 correspondence letters, and the paywalled Lancet Oncology comments on ClarIDHy, where the cost-of-benefit point is reported second-hand and should be treated as provisional. Third, SWOG S0809 was first cited as quoted by BSG 2023; its primary report (Ben-Josef, J Clin Oncol 2015, PMID 25964250) was read in full on 29 October 2026, and the non-PubMed sources — NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026, OPTN Policy 9, the OPTN review-board guidance, the UTHealth protocol v2, the HOPE4LIVER one-year update, the roadmap itself and its alignment worksheet — were read as documents but not abstracted or critiqued in the same way. Where a figure in the earlier draft could not be traced to any of these sources it has been replaced with one that can, and the removals are visible in the text: the reported incidence split for IDH1 between intrahepatic and extrahepatic disease, and a per-site adjuvant hazard ratio for hilar tumours, are both gone. Built from the Memorial Hermann Perihilar Cholangiocarcinoma System Roadmap, Draft v0.6, dated 4 October 2026 (with the liver-directed treatment revision of 3 October 2026), and its companion Guideline alignment worksheet of the same version and date, which compares AASLD 2023, BSG 2023, the ESMO 2024 interim update, the Asia-Pacific 2024 consensus, OPTN policy and review-board guidance, and NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026 (10 March 2026) across sixteen areas. The decision points follow the roadmap's own sequence: §2 (its clinical decision 0, drainage), §3 (define the extent), §4 and §4.1 (tissue and route), §5 (its clinical decision 1, resectable disease), §6 (its clinical decision 2, the transplant protocol), and §7 (its Decision points 3 and 4). Allocation criteria are from OPTN Policy 9.5.A and 9.4.C–E, official PDF checked 1 October 2026, with the programme's own standard perihilar CCA protocol v2 (policy review 16 July 2026). Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma is included in the shared liver-directed therapy matrix. The matrix link provides the current cross-disease comparison. This revision changed grades as well as numbers. Forty-five evidence strings were rewritten and twenty-seven of them were regraded downward where the full-text critique did not support the grade assigned from study design, and the reason is given in each string's note; the page now carries one grade-A string where it previously carried seven. No recommendation was removed: the roadmap's positions stand, and the page's job is to say how well supported each one is. This page reproduces a draft pending multidisciplinary and institutional governance review: it is not active clinical policy, it does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use." }

All 39 PubMed-indexed references were read in full and abstracted with an independent critique: 19 from the perihilar cholangiocarcinoma depot and 20 shared papers drawn from the intrahepatic CCA depot, which supplies the biliary systemic-therapy trials (ABC-02, TOPAZ-1, KEYNOTE-966, ABC-06, BILCAP, BCAT, PRODIGE-12, ASCOT), the targeted-therapy trials (ClarIDHy, FIGHT-202, FOENIX-CCA2, ROAR, HERIZON-BTC-01), the hepatic arterial infusion trial, the AASLD, BSG, ESMO 2023 and ESMO 2024 interim guidelines, and the two next-generation sequencing studies from the developing centre. Third, SWOG S0809 was first cited as quoted by BSG 2023; its primary report (Ben-Josef, J Clin Oncol 2015, PMID 25964250) was read in full on 29 October 2026, and the non-PubMed sources — NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026, OPTN Policy 9, the OPTN review-board guidance, the UTHealth protocol v2, the HOPE4LIVER one-year update, the roadmap itself and its alignment worksheet — were read as documents but not abstracted or critiqued in the same way. Where a figure in the earlier draft could not be traced to any of these sources it has been replaced with one that can, and the removals are visible in the text: the reported incidence split for IDH1 between intrahepatic and extrahepatic disease, and a per-site adjuvant hazard ratio for hilar tumours, are both gone. Built from the Memorial Hermann Perihilar Cholangiocarcinoma System Roadmap, Draft v0.6, dated 4 October 2026 (with the liver-directed treatment revision of 3 October 2026), and its companion Guideline alignment worksheet of the same version and date, which compares AASLD 2023, BSG 2023, the ESMO 2024 interim update, the Asia-Pacific 2024 consensus, OPTN policy and review-board guidance, and NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026 (10 March 2026) across sixteen areas. The decision points follow the roadmap's own sequence: §2 (its clinical decision 0, drainage), §3 (define the extent), §4 and §4.1 (tissue and route), §5 (its clinical decision 1, resectable disease), §6 (its clinical decision 2, the transplant protocol), and §7 (its Decision points 3 and 4). Allocation criteria are from OPTN Policy 9.5.A and 9.4.C–E, official PDF checked 1 October 2026, with the programme's own standard perihilar CCA protocol v2 (policy review 16 July 2026). Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma is included in the shared liver-directed therapy matrix. The matrix link provides the current cross-disease comparison. This revision changed grades as well as numbers. Forty-five evidence strings were rewritten and twenty-seven of them were regraded downward where the full-text critique did not support the grade assigned from study design, and the reason is given in each string's note; the page now carries one grade-A string where it previously carried seven. No recommendation was removed: the roadmap's positions stand, and the page's job is to say how well supported each one is. This page reproduces a draft pending multidisciplinary and institutional governance review: it is not active clinical policy, it does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use." }

{
  "key": "icca",
  "short": "iCCA",
  "name": "Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma",
  "version": "v0.8",
  "batch": "Batch 09, 15 October 2026",
  "lead": "Confirm the diagnosis, describe the number and distribution of liver tumors, stage the disease, and assess resection, systemic treatment, liver-directed therapy, and protocol-based transplantation.",
  "gatelabel": "Clinical decisions",
  "gates": [
    {
      "id": "1",
      "tone": "cure",
      "name": "1 · Confirm diagnosis and stage disease",
      "req": "all",
      "crit": [
        "Histology consistent with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, or a high-suspicion mass accepted for direct resection after multidisciplinary HPB review",
        "Multiphase CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis plus liver MRI with cholangiographic (MRCP) sequences, completed before any stent is placed",
        "Another primary excluded — colonoscopy, age-appropriate breast imaging and a CK7/CK20/CDX2-type panel as indicated",
        "Perihilar and distal cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancer require their own treatment assessment. Mixed HCC-iCCA has a separate combined-tumor roadmap; NLRB transplant guidance groups it with iCCA (see clinical decision 10).",
        "Recorded: tumour number and size, vascular and biliary involvement, nodal status, extrahepatic sites, ECOG, Child-Pugh and bilirubin, CA 19-9 and CEA, hepatitis serology"
      ],
      "ask": "Is the diagnosis established, and have all liver lesions, lymph nodes, and distant sites been assessed?",
      "standard": [
        {
          "t": "There is no imaging-only diagnosis of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma: unlike hepatocellular carcinoma, where LR-5 imaging in an at-risk population is diagnostic, histologic confirmation is required before systemic therapy or a tissue-defined transplant assessment; selected clearly resectable masses may proceed directly to surgery after multidisciplinary review.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "B",
          "refs": [
            "nccn",
            "36083140",
            "37770126",
            "37084797",
            "mhroadmap"
          ],
          "pref": "Every patient whose next step is systemic therapy, trial entry or tissue-defined transplant assessment — in those destinations the tissue criteria are not optional, and transplant assessment additionally needs the biopsy to grade differentiation and to exclude a mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma.",
          "avoid": "Do not demand a core from a high-suspicion, clearly resectable mass as a universal rule. NCCN states a suspicious mass on imaging in the proper clinical setting should be treated as malignant, and multidisciplinary HPB review may permit direct resection; the roadmap replaces universal pre-treatment biopsy with destination-specific confirmation.",
          "note": "AASLD 2023 and BSG 2023 require histological confirmation and LCSGJ 2022 regards biopsy as basically unnecessary for a typical resectable mass, so whether a core stays mandatory before resection is a local approval item (alignment worksheet, area 1). CEA and CA 19-9 are baseline and monitoring tests and never establish the diagnosis; CA 19-9 rises with biliary obstruction or cholangitis, so record it alongside the bilirubin and repeat it once the obstruction is relieved."
        },
        {
          "t": "Complete staging and biliary imaging before non-emergency instrumentation. Measure the future liver remnant when major hepatectomy is being considered.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "B",
          "refs": [
            "nccn",
            "37770126",
            "37084797"
          ],
          "pref": "Any patient with a tumour obstructing the biliary tree who might be resected — reactive change from a stent obscures ductal extent, which is exactly what decides whether biliary resection and reconstruction are needed. MRI is the study that characterises the biliary and vascular relationships that determine resectability, and EASL-ILCA prefers it over CT for intrahepatic staging.",
          "avoid": "Do not wait for imaging in cholangitis — that is drained without waiting for the discussion, and urgent sepsis treatment takes priority over the elective sequence.",
          "note": "Where the tumour obstructs the biliary tree, the need for drainage, its route and its side are decided with the hepatobiliary surgeon before any non-emergency procedure; resection without preoperative drainage can be considered when the future remnant is large. That drainage rule is grade D on its own — no comparative outcome data in intrahepatic disease were identified for it — while the grade B on this string covers the imaging sequence, which BSG 2023 and EASL-ILCA both recommend."
        },
        {
          "t": "Exclude another primary before committing to this pathway, because metastatic adenocarcinoma can be histologically indistinguishable from intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "D",
          "refs": [
            "mhroadmap"
          ],
          "pref": "Any adenocarcinoma in the liver without an established primary, and particularly before a patient is started on a biliary-tract regimen or entered into a biliary trial.",
          "avoid": "Do not let the immunohistochemical panel consume the whole core: BSG 2023 asks that tissue be reserved for molecular profiling when immunohistochemistry is planned, and whether to add that instruction is a local approval item (alignment worksheet, area 12).",
          "note": "Treating a colorectal or pancreatic metastasis as intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is a recognised and consequential error. Hepatitis B and C status and any cirrhosis are established at entry: they change operative risk and, where a mixed tumour is possible, the differential."
        },
        {
          "t": "Describe every suspected tumor nodule by number, size, liver segment, and relationship to the main tumor. Distinguish liver-confined multifocal disease from regional nodal involvement and distant metastases.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "D",
          "refs": [
            "capicca",
            "rcpafocality",
            "41172153"
          ],
          "pref": "Use the definitions in the “Multiple liver tumors” reference above. Confirm whether additional lesions are malignant when that uncertainty would change treatment.",
          "avoid": "Do not label all additional liver nodules as distant stage IV disease, assume satellites are harmless, or infer independent primary tumors from imaging alone.",
          "note": "The descriptions overlap biologically. Record imaging uncertainty and obtain expert radiology/pathology review rather than assigning a treatment solely from the label."
        }
      ],
      "alt": [
        {
          "t": "Plan molecular testing of a dedicated biliary specimen at the index ERCP where the disease presents as an indeterminate stricture rather than a mass and the alternative is a repeat procedure.",
          "l": "Reasonable",
          "g": "C",
          "refs": [
            "41905432",
            "30971436"
          ],
          "pref": "The patient entering the pathway as an indeterminate stricture, where pathology alone is weakest: in a 6-year prospective study of 2,116 patients across 28 institutions, pathologic assessment of ERCP brushings and biopsies had 44% sensitivity overall and 36% for intrahepatic or hilar strictures, while a DNA/RNA sequencing panel on separately collected specimens in a dedicated nucleic-acid buffer reached 82% sensitivity at 98% specificity and the combination 88% at 97%. Specificity was 99% for pathology, so sequencing bought sensitivity and gave up almost nothing.",
          "avoid": "Do not read a negative molecular result as excluding malignancy — in the original single-centre cohort there were 37 false negatives (25%) and the negative predictive value was only 63%, with sampling failure the usual explanation; in 12 of those cases the same panel found an alteration in the resected tumour. Only 2% of neoplastic strictures in the 2026 study were purely dysplastic, so outside primary sclerosing cholangitis this is earlier diagnosis of established cancer, not early detection, and no resectability or survival benefit has been shown. Payer authorisation and the dedicated collection buffer have to be arranged before the procedure, not after.",
          "note": "Correct the yield figure: therapeutically relevant alterations were reported in 20 of 150 cancers (13%) in the original single-centre cohort, and in the 2026 multi-institutional study in 137 of 458 cholangiocarcinomas (30%) — but only on the 161-gene version of the panel. The 28-gene version used in the original cohort did not detect FGFR2 fusions at all, which with chromatin-remodelling genes accounts for up to 20% of intrahepatic tumours, so a biliary specimen substitutes for the clinical decision 2 profile only if the panel actually run reports fusions. Downgraded from B: specimens were submitted at the endoscopist's discretion rather than consecutively, a stricture could be classified neoplastic on 12 months of clinical or radiographic progression rather than on tissue, and all testing was done in the laboratory that developed the assay."
        },
        {
          "t": "Add FDG-PET selectively, for suspected occult spread and for transplant staging.",
          "l": "Reasonable",
          "g": "B",
          "refs": [
            "nccn",
            "37770126",
            "37084797"
          ],
          "pref": "Where occult nodal or distant disease would change the operation, and in any patient being staged for a transplant protocol.",
          "avoid": "Do not substitute PET for MRI with MRCP in local planning; MRCP is preferred for biliary anatomy and ERCP or PTC are used more for therapeutic intervention.",
          "note": "BSG 2023 recommends FDG-PET-CT for nodal and distant disease as part of staging and EASL-ILCA recommends it routinely in apparently resectable patients, both more broadly than our selective wording — alignment worksheet, area 2. Read the strength of the broader recommendation honestly: the EASL-ILCA routine-PET statement passed its Delphi panel with only 78% agreement, the weakest consensus in that guideline's staging section, and AASLD 2023 states PET should not be used to assess the primary tumour."
        }
      ],
      "avoid": [
        {
          "t": "Do not place a biliary stent in a potentially resectable patient before the biliary-protocol imaging is complete and the drainage plan is agreed with the hepatobiliary surgeon.",
          "l": "Avoid",
          "g": "D",
          "refs": [
            "nccn",
            "37770126"
          ],
          "pref": "The only exception is cholangitis, which is drained immediately.",
          "avoid": "Stent-related inflammation obscures ductal extent, and drainage of the wrong side or an unnecessary procedure adds cholangitis risk and can delay both surgery and systemic therapy."
        },
        {
          "t": "Do not assign this pathway to perihilar or distal cholangiocarcinoma — the drainage problem, the operation and the transplant question all differ.",
          "l": "Avoid",
          "g": "D",
          "refs": [
            "mhroadmap"
          ],
          "pref": "Use the separate perihilar roadmap; gallbladder cancer, mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma and paediatric disease are out of scope here.",
          "avoid": "In particular, the standardised perihilar MELD exception and its neoadjuvant/stricture protocol do not transfer to intrahepatic disease."
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "2",
      "tone": "sys",
      "name": "2 · Request molecular profiling",
      "req": "any",
      "crit": [
        "Unresectable or metastatic disease at diagnosis — order now, not at the point of second-line progression",
        "Borderline or locally advanced disease where systemic therapy is the first step",
        "Recurrence after resection that will be treated systemically",
        "Adequate tissue preserved from the diagnostic core, or plasma where tissue is inadequate or a biopsy would delay treatment"
      ],
      "ask": "Has molecular profiling been requested in time to guide treatment?",
      "standard": [
        {
          "t": "Order broad molecular profiling at the diagnosis of unresectable or metastatic disease, not at the point of second-line progression.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "B",
          "refs": [
            "nccn",
            "39864891",
            "37770126",
            "36083140",
            "42312290"
          ],
          "pref": "Everyone who will receive systemic therapy. The rationale is operational rather than biological: turnaround is typically two to four weeks, and a patient who progresses on first-line chemo-immunotherapy needs the result in hand at that moment.",
          "avoid": "Ordering it at progression means the second-line decision is made without it, and the default becomes FOLFOX by omission rather than by choice. The obstacle here is payer authorisation and ordering discipline, not the clinical argument.",
          "note": "Our grade B is lower than ESMO 2024's [I, A] and BSG 2023's strong recommendation on high-quality evidence. ILTS-ILCA 2024 recommends comprehensive sequencing in unresectable or metastatic iCCA but finds no evidence for using it to select transplant candidates. Capture NRG1 and other actionable findings on the same panel; do not label each matched agent category 1 merely because testing is recommended."
        },
        {
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "C",
          "opts": [
            {
              "name": "FGFR2 fusion or rearrangement",
              "g": "C",
              "when": "Preferred for a defined phenotype. Pemigatinib after prior systemic therapy, or futibatinib after gemcitabine–platinum. At final FIGHT-202 analysis, independently reviewed response was 37.0% with median progression-free survival 7.0 months and median overall survival 17.5 months in 108 patients; FOENIX-CCA2 gave response 42%, median progression-free survival 9.0 months and median overall survival 21.7 months in 103 patients.",
              "pref": "Second line or later in a patient fit for an oral targeted agent, where the alteration reported is a fusion or rearrangement — 90% of FIGHT-202 and the whole of FOENIX-CCA2 was intrahepatic disease, so this is the alteration with the most directly applicable data.",
              "avoid": "Do not infer superiority over second-line chemotherapy: both trials are single-arm, neither has been compared with it, and The pemigatinib investigators explicitly warn against the cross-study comparison with pooled second-line chemotherapy (response 9.5%, progression-free survival 2.6 months) that makes the agent look better. Both drugs were approved on these single-arm data. Do not expect the alteration in an untested patient — 783 patients were screened to enrol 103 in FOENIX-CCA2, and 1,206 were prescreened to find 107 fusion-positive patients for FIGHT-202.",
              "note": "At the FIGHT-202 final analysis there were no objective responses in the cohorts with other FGF/FGFR alterations (0 of 20) or with none (0 of 17), so the effect is confined to the fusion and rearrangement class; with 20 and 17 patients that is a weak negative rather than proof. Hyperphosphataemia affected 58.5% on pemigatinib and 85% on futibatinib (grade 3 in 30%), and acquired kinase-domain resistance mutations emerged in those who shrank then progressed. Benefit is modest in absolute terms and FIGHT-302 has reported (PMID 42223137): 167 randomized patients, PFS 8.3 versus 6.8 months with pemigatinib versus GemCis (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.39–0.87; nominal P=.0078), without demonstrated OS benefit (24.4 versus 25.0 months). The trial closed early, permitted substantial crossover and did not compare against chemo-immunotherapy; it does not by itself establish a new first-line policy.",
              "refs": [
                "38838500",
                "32203698",
                "36652354",
                "42223137"
              ]
            },
            {
              "name": "IDH1 mutation",
              "g": "B",
              "when": "Preferred for a defined phenotype, positioned on progression-free survival grounds only. ClarIDHy met its primary endpoint — median progression-free survival 2.7 versus 1.4 months, hazard ratio 0.37 — but the final intention-to-treat overall survival was 10.3 versus 7.5 months, hazard ratio 0.79 (95% CI 0.56–1.12), p=0.09, not significant, with 70% of placebo patients crossing over.",
              "pref": "A chemotherapy-refractory patient with an IDH1 mutation who understands that the benefit is disease stabilisation: objective response was 2% and the signal came from stable disease, 51% versus 28%. Physical functioning was better preserved than on placebo.",
              "avoid": "Do not promise surgical conversion: objective response was only 2%, and the trial did not test a conversion or transplant strategy. A response may still warrant MDT reassessment. The final crossover-adjusted OS estimate is model-dependent and, after the October 2026 correction, is HR 0.49 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.25–1.24), not a significant randomized survival result.",
              "note": "The comparator was placebo, not the active second-line standard, so the gain over mFOLFOX is unknown. Note the population when reading this into a liver pathway: only 9 of 185 patients (5%) had cirrhosis, 93% were metastatic and 90% of the ivosidenib arm had intrahepatic disease, so this is a non-cirrhotic metastatic cohort and nothing like a transplant or conversion candidate. Quality-of-life conclusions rest on change scores available for 62 of 113 ivosidenib and 20 of 52 placebo patients.",
              "refs": [
                "32416072",
                "34554208"
              ]
            },
            {
              "name": "BRAF V600E",
              "g": "C",
              "when": "Preferred for a defined phenotype. Dabrafenib plus trametinib: single-arm, 43 patients, response 51% by investigator and 47% by independent review, median progression-free survival 9 months and median overall survival 14 months — interim analysis.",
              "pref": "A previously treated patient with a centrally confirmable V600E mutation; 39 of the 43 patients (91%) had intrahepatic disease, so the population matches.",
              "avoid": "Do not expect the trial's 9% screening yield in practice — several sites entered already-known positives and the real rate is nearer 5–7%. Patients with bilirubin above three times normal or untreatable biliary obstruction were excluded, so this says nothing about the jaundiced patient.",
              "refs": [
                "32818466"
              ]
            },
            {
              "name": "HER2 amplification or overexpression",
              "g": "C",
              "when": "Preferred for a defined phenotype. Zanidatamab: single-arm; at final analysis (median follow-up 33.4 months, 80 ERBB2-amplified patients) confirmed response was 41% (33 of 80, 95% CI 30–53) and median overall survival 15.5 months.",
              "pref": "An IHC 3+ tumour, where the activity is concentrated: response 52% (32 of 62) versus 6% (1 of 18) at IHC 2+, disease control 79% versus 33%, and median overall survival 18.1 versus 5.2 months — a post hoc split the authors themselves label as such.",
              "avoid": "Do not offer it on an IHC 2+ result as though the trial supported it, and do not read the 15.5-month survival as attributable to the drug: there was no control group and 44% of patients received further anticancer therapy afterwards.",
              "note": "Results are reported for biliary tract cancer as a whole with no breakdown by subsite, so the effect specifically in intrahepatic disease is unknown; HER2 is a minority of iCCA. ESMO 2024 also recommends considering trastuzumab deruxtecan for HER2 overexpression or amplification, which our table does not name — alignment worksheet, area 14.",
              "refs": [
                "41264278",
                "39864891"
              ]
            },
            {
              "name": "MSI-high or mismatch-repair deficient",
              "g": "C",
              "when": "Preferred for a defined phenotype. Checkpoint blockade, consistent with tumour-agnostic practice.",
              "pref": "The small hypermutated subset — and it is small: only 5 of 333 evaluable patients in TOPAZ-1 and 10 in KEYNOTE-966 were MSI-high.",
              "avoid": "Do not recycle checkpoint blockade without accounting for prior exposure to first-line durvalumab or pembrolizumab.",
              "refs": [
                "nccn",
                "38319896",
                "37075781"
              ]
            },
            {
              "name": "NTRK fusion, RET fusion, other actionable alterations",
              "g": "C",
              "when": "Reasonable consideration. Capture on the same broad panel so a later line is not delayed by re-testing.",
              "pref": "Any patient being profiled — the panel costs nothing extra and removes a re-testing delay.",
              "avoid": "Do not treat capture as a licence to prescribe: ESMO 2024 recommends NTRK inhibitors and selpercatinib for RET fusions on level III evidence, while our table only requires that these alterations be captured. Whether to name the agents is a local approval item.",
              "refs": [
                "39864891"
              ]
            }
          ],
          "order": "Match treatment to the actionable alteration and prior therapy; this order does not establish a sequence. ClarIDHy provides randomized second-line IDH1 evidence and FIGHT-302 provides a separate first-line FGFR2 comparison against GemCis without immunotherapy. Both demonstrated PFS benefit without a demonstrated ITT OS advantage. The other registration studies listed here are principally single-arm response studies; cross-trial results do not establish comparative survival.",
          "flagnote": "Match treatment to the alteration class reported, not to the gene name. The evidence above is for FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements, IDH1 mutation, BRAF V600E, HER2 amplification or overexpression, and MSI-high or mismatch-repair deficiency; other alterations in the same genes are not interchangeable and should be reviewed with a clinician experienced in molecular oncology before a matched agent is chosen — Standard, grade D. Whether the HER2 row names trastuzumab deruxtecan and the NTRK/RET row names agents, as ESMO 2024 does, is a local approval item (alignment worksheet, area 14)."
        }
      ],
      "alt": [
        {
          "t": "Use circulating tumour DNA when tissue is inadequate or the biopsy would delay treatment.",
          "l": "Reasonable",
          "g": "C",
          "refs": [
            "37770126",
            "36652354"
          ],
          "pref": "The patient whose core is exhausted or whose repeat biopsy would push the start of treatment out by weeks.",
          "avoid": "Do not accept a negative plasma result as excluding a target — BSG 2023 notes DNA-based panels and most liquid biopsies are weaker at detecting fusions, so a negative plasma result should prompt tissue testing where it would change management.",
          "note": "Read the plasma figure for what it is: the FGFR2 fusion or rearrangement was detectable in plasma in 83 of 95 FOENIX-CCA2 patients tested (87%), but those patients were already known to be tissue-positive, so 87% is concordance in a positive population and not the chance of finding a target de novo in an unselected patient. No study in this disease reports the latter."
        }
      ],
      "avoid": [
        {
          "t": "Do not defer profiling to the point of second-line progression.",
          "l": "Avoid",

  "provenance": "Website language revised 23 October 2026 to use direct clinical questions and consistent terminology. The focality clarification additionally uses CAP intrahepatic bile-duct protocol v4.3 (June 2025), EASL–ILCA 2023 and current OPTN NLRB guidance. Wei 2025 (PMID 41172153) has since been read in full; it does not establish equivalence, operative superiority or an adopted staging change. Revised 7 October 2026 (Batch 08) after a full-text read of this page's reference depot: 37 structured abstracts, each carrying the authors' own stated limitations and an independent critique with its sources identified, against which every evidence string on this page was rechecked for the published number, for whether the critique undercuts what the string claims, and for whether the grade still follows. Thirty-three evidence strings changed. Three grades were lowered and the reason is recorded in each note: first-line chemo-immunotherapy in permanently unresectable liver-confined disease from A to B, because TOPAZ-1 and KEYNOTE-966 were 86% and 89% metastatic and say nothing about this population; offering adjuvant capecitabine from B to C, because BILCAP did not meet its intention-to-treat primary endpoint and only 19% of its patients had intrahepatic disease; and sequencing a dedicated biliary specimen at ERCP from B to C, because specimens were submitted non-consecutively, the reference standard allowed clinical and radiographic progression in place of tissue, and all testing was done in the laboratory that developed the assay. The transplant assessment was corrected most: the international explant series is now cited only for what it studied — 15 patients with single tumours of 2 cm or less, diagnosed on explant pathology, with mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma excluded and no requirement for disease stability on therapy — and the 3 cm ceiling and the six-month stability period in our criteria are attributed to EASL-ILCA, the OPTN review-board guidance and ILTS-ILCA rather than to that series. The ILTS-ILCA 2024 consensus is published twice and both records are cited (PMID 40014003, Liver Transplantation 2025; PMID 42312290, Liver Cancer 2026); the ESMO 2023 parent guideline (PMID 36372281) is now cited alongside its 2024 interim update, since the update covers only molecular diagnostics and advanced disease and leaves the surgical recommendations to the parent. Every reference the page cites was read in full. Still cited from the source document rather than from a full-text read: NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026, OPTN Policy 9 and the OPTN Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology guidance (December 2025), the Memorial Hermann roadmap and its alignment worksheet, and the HOPE4LIVER one-year histotripsy update, which in any case enrolled hepatocellular carcinoma and metastases rather than intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Built from the Memorial Hermann Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma System Roadmap, Draft v0.6 (4 October 2026, including the 3 October 2026 liver-directed treatment revision), and its companion Guideline alignment worksheet of the same date, which compares the roadmap against AASLD 2023, OPTN 2025 review-board guidance, ESMO 2024 interim update, BSG 2023, LCSGJ 2022, ILTS-ILCA 2024 and NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026 across 16 areas. Evidence strings carry the published numbers and the published criticism; where the roadmap's label and the trial's primary endpoint diverge, both are stated and the local approval item is named. No recommendation was removed because its evidence turned out to be weak; the roadmap's position stands and the page now says how well supported it is. The liver-directed therapy matrix is read directly from the shared matrix file and is not reproduced here. This page reproduces a draft pending multidisciplinary approval: it is not active clinical policy, does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use. HAI sections updated 15 October 2026 to Batch 09. New studies were checked against indexed abstracts and the published ASCO abstract; new full-text PDFs remain to be acquired. No new full-text review is claimed for these additions."
}

The focality clarification additionally uses CAP intrahepatic bile-duct protocol v4.3 (June 2025), EASL–ILCA 2023 and current OPTN NLRB guidance. Wei 2025 (PMID 41172153) has since been read in full; it does not establish equivalence, operative superiority or an adopted staging change. Revised 7 October 2026 (Batch 08) after a full-text read of this page's reference depot: 37 structured abstracts, each carrying the authors' own stated limitations and an independent critique with its sources identified, against which every evidence string on this page was rechecked for the published number, for whether the critique undercuts what the string claims, and for whether the grade still follows. Thirty-three evidence strings changed. Three grades were lowered and the reason is recorded in each note: first-line chemo-immunotherapy in permanently unresectable liver-confined disease from A to B, because TOPAZ-1 and KEYNOTE-966 were 86% and 89% metastatic and say nothing about this population; offering adjuvant capecitabine from B to C, because BILCAP did not meet its intention-to-treat primary endpoint and only 19% of its patients had intrahepatic disease; and sequencing a dedicated biliary specimen at ERCP from B to C, because specimens were submitted non-consecutively, the reference standard allowed clinical and radiographic progression in place of tissue, and all testing was done in the laboratory that developed the assay. The transplant assessment was corrected most: the international explant series is now cited only for what it studied — 15 patients with single tumours of 2 cm or less, diagnosed on explant pathology, with mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma excluded and no requirement for disease stability on therapy — and the 3 cm ceiling and the six-month stability period in our criteria are attributed to EASL-ILCA, the OPTN review-board guidance and ILTS-ILCA rather than to that series. The ILTS-ILCA 2024 consensus is published twice and both records are cited (PMID 40014003, Liver Transplantation 2025; PMID 42312290, Liver Cancer 2026); the ESMO 2023 parent guideline (PMID 36372281) is now cited alongside its 2024 interim update, since the update covers only molecular diagnostics and advanced disease and leaves the surgical recommendations to the parent. Every reference the page cites was read in full. Still cited from the source document rather than from a full-text read: NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026, OPTN Policy 9 and the OPTN Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology guidance (December 2025), the Memorial Hermann roadmap and its alignment worksheet, and the HOPE4LIVER one-year histotripsy update, which in any case enrolled hepatocellular carcinoma and metastases rather than intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Built from the Memorial Hermann Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma System Roadmap, Draft v0.6 (4 October 2026, including the 3 October 2026 liver-directed treatment revision), and its companion Guideline alignment worksheet of the same date, which compares the roadmap against AASLD 2023, OPTN 2025 review-board guidance, ESMO 2024 interim update, BSG 2023, LCSGJ 2022, ILTS-ILCA 2024 and NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026 across 16 areas. Evidence strings carry the published numbers and the published criticism; where the roadmap's label and the trial's primary endpoint diverge, both are stated and the local approval item is named. No recommendation was removed because its evidence turned out to be weak; the roadmap's position stands and the page now says how well supported it is. The liver-directed therapy matrix is read directly from the shared matrix file and is not reproduced here. This page reproduces a draft pending multidisciplinary approval: it is not active clinical policy, does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use. HAI sections updated 15 October 2026 to Batch 09. New studies were checked against indexed abstracts and the published ASCO abstract; new full-text PDFs remain to be acquired. No new full-text review is claimed for these additions."
}

        "Functional syndrome recorded explicitly, confirmed with directed tests",
        "Hepatic burden and distribution: unilobar versus bilobar, resectable versus diffuse-miliary",

      "standard": [
        {
          "t": "Obtain expert pathology reporting differentiation and representative Ki-67, with mitoses when evaluable. An adequate small biopsy may be graded with Ki-67 when mitoses cannot be assessed; inadequate or discordant tissue needs review and further sampling if it would change treatment.",

          "g": "C",

            "28609356",
            "36924180"

ENETS 2023 explicitly states that Ki-67 alone cannot distinguish NET G3 from NEC. Use differentiation, morphology and appropriate immunohistochemistry; 55% is not a diagnostic boundary. A mixed neuroendocrine–non-neuroendocrine neoplasm is named as such, and its clinically dominant aggressive component sets the pathway."

        {
          "t": "Stage with somatostatin-receptor PET/CT, 68Ga-DOTATATE or equivalent, alongside cross-sectional CT or MRI.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "B",
          "refs": [
            "33588146",
            "37774329"
          ],
          "pref": "Use SSTR imaging for staging and when it will change management, including PRRT assessment or discordant progression. Use CT/MRI for routine response surveillance and repeat receptor imaging selectively.",
          "avoid": "Do not use receptor uptake as a substitute for anatomic burden assessment or as a universal response measure, and do not order octreotide SPECT/CT unless SSTR-PET is unavailable.",
          "note": "Graded B on diagnostic accuracy rather than on outcome: NANETS 2017 reports 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT sensitivity of 95% against 31% for octreotide SPECT, which is why the substitution is made. The EANM position itself is a modified three-round Delphi vote — necessary at staging of all NET in 19 of 23 panellists (82.6%), CT or MRI also necessary in 20 of 23 (87.0%) — with consensus set at 70% agreement for a single answer and only 50% preference in multiple-choice format, and consensus failed on 12 of 43 questions. The panel was drawn from high-volume centres with full access to Ga-68 tracer and PRRT, so availability is assumed rather than tested. Where SSTR-PET has not been done, the board records its absence explicitly rather than proceeding as if it had."
        },
        {
          "t": "Record carcinoid syndrome, insulinoma, gastrinoma or any other functional syndrome explicitly, confirmed with tests directed at the suspected syndrome rather than a panel of every available marker.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "D",
          "refs": [
            "39266864"
          ],
          "pref": "Before any hepatic procedure — this changes procedural safety planning, not only symptom management, and high hepatic burden with a midgut primary is the dominant carcinoid-crisis risk combination.",
          "avoid": "Do not treat a normal marker panel as excluding a functional syndrome, and do not leave the syndrome undocumented because symptoms are currently controlled on an analogue.",
          "note": "Grade D: a named local requirement with no comparative outcome evidence behind the thresholds themselves."
        },
        {
          "t": "State the hepatic tumour burden, unilobar versus bilobar, resectable versus diffuse-miliary pattern, the primary site and whether it is resected, the extrahepatic sites, and which problem is driving the clinical picture.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "D",
          "pref": "Every case at submission: burden and distribution decide whether cytoreduction, embolotherapy or transplantation is an option at all.",
          "avoid": "Do not open a treatment discussion where the dominant problem has not been named — hormonal symptoms and tumour progression need different answers and conflating them produces treatment without an endpoint."

      "alt": [
        {
          "t": "Obtain FDG PET where the grade is high, where behaviour is discordant with grade, where SSTR uptake is heterogeneous, or where a CT or MRI lesion shows no SSTR uptake.",
          "l": "Reasonable",
          "g": "B",
          "refs": [
            "33588146",
            "39395114"

          "pref": "Before committing to receptor-directed therapy in G2–G3 disease or rapid progression, to find receptor-negative, FDG-avid disease that PRRT will not treat.",

          "note": "The roadmap keeps FDG selective on the Itanet triggers rather than requiring it for every G2–G3 PRRT candidate as EANM Focus 3 does. EANM endorsed FDG before PRRT in G2–G3 to exclude mismatched FDG-positive, SSTR-negative lesions in 19 of 23 panellists (82.6%) by modified Delphi, and Itanet grades the FDG trigger 3b-A. What neither establishes is that acting on the mismatch changes outcome: EANM's extension of PRRT into G3 rests on two small retrospective series confined to Ki-67 under 55%, and EANM reached no consensus at all on PRRT with mismatched lesions."

          "t": "Consider re-biopsy on unexpected behavioural change or discordant FDG avidity.",
          "l": "Reasonable",
          "g": "C",
          "refs": [
            "39395114"

          "pref": "Where the original grading is years old or the disease has clearly changed pace: grade progression and transformation both occur and change the pathway.",
          "avoid": "Not as a scheduled ritual — no study defines the trigger or the interval, which is why this sits at C and remains an open local decision.",

        {
          "t": "Do not assign a pathway on grade alone.",
          "l": "Avoid",
          "g": "D",
          "pref": "The differentiation fork drives every later decision, so the tissue standard is deliberately set high.",
          "avoid": "If differentiation cannot be established on the available material, get more material rather than guessing from Ki-67."

        {
          "t": "Do not manage a poorly differentiated carcinoma on the indolent-disease pathway.",
          "l": "Avoid",
          "g": "B",

          "pref": "Carcinoma is managed as an aggressive carcinoma. In the SEER figures ENETS 2023 reproduces, median survival is 33.9 months for stage I–II, 16.3 months for stage III and 5.2 months for distant disease, with 5-year survival 42%, 25.6% and 4.7%; metastatic patients survive a median 11 to 12 months on palliative platinum–etoposide and about 1 month without it. Performance status then dominates: median survival 18 months at PS 0, 12 at PS 1 and 5 at PS 2.",
          "avoid": "Somatostatin analogue for antiproliferative intent, PRRT, hepatic debulking for cytoreduction and transplantation are all inappropriate here. Managing a carcinoma on the indolent pathway costs months of ineffective therapy in a disease measured in months. Note what the recommendation is made of: ENETS grades both the advice against metastasectomy and the advice against PRRT in metastatic digestive NEC 5D, its weakest grade, resting on no comparative data, and well-differentiated G3 NET is outside that paper's scope by design — so the guidance is strongest exactly where the diagnosis is unambiguous and silent where it is not."

    {
      "id": "2",
      "tone": "sys",

            "25014687",
            "38977327"

The effect is stabilisation, not shrinkage: one partial remission per arm in PROMID, and objective remissions with an analogue are rare. For a liver pathway the decisive limitation is that PROMID's exploratory burden subgroups had imprecise estimates and did not establish a predictive liver-volume threshold — hazard ratio 0.17 (0.08–0.40) at 0 to 10% hepatic involvement, 0.40 (0.10–1.67) at 10 to 50% and 0.71 (0.11–4.45) above 50%, with 95% of patients having Ki-67 of 2% or less and 64/85 (75%) having 10% or less liver involvement, including those without liver disease. For carcinoid-syndrome control the source is ENETS 2024, not these trials."
        }
      ],

        {
          "l": "Reasonable",
          "g": "B",

The three thresholds do not agree with one another and none was derived.",

The CLARINET placebo arm itself ran a median 18.0 months without progression.",
              "avoid": "Not where the syndrome is active, where receptor-positive bulk is accumulating, or where the patient will not reliably return for imaging. The 3–4-month interval is a local choice within the NCCN range of every 12 weeks to 12 months.",

                "37774329",
                "38977327"

                "34793718",
                "32015164",
                "39395114"
              ]
            },

  "provenance": "Built from the Memorial Hermann Neuroendocrine Liver Metastasis System Roadmap, Draft v0.6 dated 4 October 2026 with its liver-directed therapy section revised 3 October 2026, and from the companion guideline alignment worksheet of the same date, which compares the roadmap against NCCN Neuroendocrine and Adrenal Tumors v1.2026 (21 April 2026), NANETS 2017 medical and surgical consensus statements, NANETS 2020 surgical consensus, EANM Focus 3 (2021), Itanet 2024, ENETS 2023–2024 guidance and the OPTN National Liver Review Board transplant-oncology guidance of December 2025 against OPTN Policy 9 as checked on 1 October 2026. One figure on the page is cited from a guideline rather than from the paper itself and was not read in full: the Maire 2012 randomised TAE versus TACE trial of 26 patients, quoted from ENETS. The NCCN guideline, the OPTN policy and review-board guidance, the HOPE4LIVER update, the Memorial Hermann roadmap and its alignment worksheet are not PubMed-indexed depot papers and were read as documents; the ASCO 2025 symptom-management guideline is PubMed-indexed (PMID 40344544) but was outside the depot and was read as a document. The liver-directed therapy matrix is rendered from the shared modality matrix, which is outside this page's scope and which carries RETNET outcome figures the protocol paper does not report; approval item 12 assigns its correction. Both source documents are drafts pending multidisciplinary and institutional governance review: they are not active clinical policy, do not replace clinician judgement, current drug labelling, OPTN policy or patient-specific informed consent, and every numeric criterion must be verified against its current source before use."

  "provenance": "Built from the Memorial Hermann Neuroendocrine Liver Metastasis System Roadmap, Draft v0.6 dated 4 October 2026 with its liver-directed therapy section revised 3 October 2026, and from the companion guideline alignment worksheet of the same date, which compares the roadmap against NCCN Neuroendocrine and Adrenal Tumors v1.2026 (21 April 2026), NANETS 2017 medical and surgical consensus statements, NANETS 2020 surgical consensus, EANM Focus 3 (2021), Itanet 2024, ENETS 2023–2024 guidance and the OPTN National Liver Review Board transplant-oncology guidance of December 2025 against OPTN Policy 9 as checked on 1 October 2026. Revised on 7 October 2026 (Batch 08) after a full-text read of the whole NELM reference depot: 33 papers, each carrying an independently recorded critique, covering all 33 PubMed-indexed references cited on this page. Every evidence string was re-checked against each paper's own reported results rather than against a guideline quoting it, and grades were re-set where the full text showed a recommendation resting on a surrogate endpoint, a cohort with no comparator arm, an unvalidated threshold or a consensus vote; 40 evidence strings changed and 4 grades were lowered in that pass, and the limited-evidence section was rewritten and expanded from 9 entries to 34 with six further local approval items added. Four references are cited partly or wholly for what they do not show: RETNET (PMID 30016989) is a published protocol with no outcome data, so no efficacy figure on this page rests on it and the drug-eluting-bead arm closure is attributed to the ENETS 2024 guidance that reports it; the ENETS 2023 digestive neuroendocrine carcinoma paper is cited for a recommendation it grades 5D; NANETS 2017 medical and NANETS 2020 surgical are cited in several places for recorded absences of consensus. One figure on the page is cited from a guideline rather than from the paper itself and was not read in full: the Maire 2012 randomised TAE versus TACE trial of 26 patients, quoted from ENETS. The NCCN guideline, the OPTN policy and review-board guidance, the HOPE4LIVER update, the Memorial Hermann roadmap and its alignment worksheet are not PubMed-indexed depot papers and were read as documents; the ASCO 2025 symptom-management guideline is PubMed-indexed (PMID 40344544) but was outside the depot and was read as a document. The shared liver-directed therapy matrix now distinguishes the RETNET 2018 protocol from the NANETS 2025 conference results. The attribution correction is complete (NELM-D12); retrieval of a final full-text efficacy report and subsequent source-version checks remain separate maintenance tasks. Both source documents are drafts pending multidisciplinary and institutional governance review: they are not active clinical policy, do not replace clinician judgement, current drug labelling, OPTN policy or patient-specific informed consent, and every numeric criterion must be verified against its current source before use."

NCCN reports that re-imaging patients who arrived with a non-pancreas-protocol CT changed the stage and the management in 56% of cases at a single institution, and that where CT showed a resectable tumour 70% to 85% of patients went on to resection. Both figures are NCCN's citation of single-institution series and are not in the reporting-template paper this item is referenced to.", "avoid": "Do not accept thick sections, positive oral contrast or a single post-contrast phase. Neutral oral contrast only, because positive contrast degrades the 3D and maximum-intensity-projection reformats that show the vessels. Sections as thin as the scanner allows, under 3 mm and preferably submillimetre, reconstructed at 2–3 mm with multiplanar reformats.", "note": "Accuracy decays with time because the disease moves: NCCN prefers imaging within four weeks of surgery; reassess timing in context rather than using it as an absolute initial-review exclusion. Sensitivity for small hepatic and peritoneal deposits is limited however good the protocol is, and protocol quality is not the whole of the problem — in SWOG S1505, 43 of 146 patients centrally reviewed (29%) did not meet the trial's own resectability criteria, 51% of them for arterial interface and 65% for suspicion of distant disease, and adding a mandatory site radiologist checklist moved that only from 33% to 26%. [EXPERTISE]" }, { "t": "Report it against the Society of Abdominal Radiology and American Pancreatic Association template, in degrees of vessel contact — not in adjectives.", "l": "Standard", "g": "D", "refs": [ "24354378" ], "pref": "Every staging report. {
 "key": "pnet",
 "short": "PNET",
 "name": "Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, primary",
 "version": "v0.2",
 "batch": "Batch 08, 7 October 2026",
 "lead": "Use differentiation, grade, hormone production, disease extent, and surgical risk to select surveillance or treatment of a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.",
 "gatelabel": "Clinical decisions",
 "gates": [
  {
   "id": "1",
   "tone": "cure",
   "name": "1 · Confirm differentiation and grade",
   "req": "all",
   "crit": [
    "Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumour, not a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma",
    "Exact Ki-67 index and mitotic rate per 2 mm² when assessable; document tissue adequacy and use Ki-67 when a small biopsy cannot support a reliable mitotic count",
    "Two of synaptophysin, chromogranin A and INSM1 positive, with a broad-spectrum keratin",
    "Acinar cell carcinoma and the other neuroendocrine-marker mimics excluded where the morphology is unusual",
    "Functional status recorded as a clinical and biochemical judgement, not an immunohistochemical one"
   ],
   "ask": "Are differentiation, grade, and the measured Ki-67 index established?",
   "standard": [
    {
     "t": "Report differentiation, exact Ki-67 and mitotic rate per 2 mm² when assessable. Record specimen adequacy; a reliable Ki-67-based grade can be used when mitotic counting is not possible.",
     "l": "Standard",
     "g": "B",
     "refs": [
      "31856076",
      "37877341"
     ],
     "pref": "Every specimen, primary or metastatic, biopsy or resection, with at least 500 assessable tumour cells and no crush artefact. Ki-67 is counted in the hot spot of highest nuclear labelling; the mitotic rate is counted in the areas of highest density, per 2 mm², which equals 10 high-power fields at 40× with a 0.5 mm ocular field.",
     "avoid": "Do not accept a report that says \"neuroendocrine tumour\" or \"neuroendocrine carcinoma\" without a grade and without the parameters used to assign it. NCCN states plainly that such a report is inadequate for prognostication and therapy and inappropriate for pathology reporting.",
     "note": "Where mitotic rate and Ki-67 give different grades, the higher grade is assigned. Where several blocks are available, stain the block with the highest mitotic index and grade on the highest index; with synchronous specimens from several sites, stain at least one block from each."
    },
    {
     "t": "Separate a well-differentiated grade 3 tumour from a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma before any treatment decision — they are different diseases that share a Ki-67 range.",
     "l": "Standard",
     "g": "C",
     "refs": [
      "26482044",
      "31856076",
      "36924180"
     ],
     "pref": "Any pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasm with Ki-67 above 20%. In 31 well-differentiated tumours with a morphologically apparent high-grade component, 21 of them pancreatic, median disease-specific survival was 55 months (range 16-119), with 2-year and 5-year survival of 88-89% and 48-49%. The institutional comparators were 162 months for low and intermediate grade pancreatic well-differentiated tumours (2-year and 5-year 97% and 90%) and 16 months for pancreatic poorly differentiated carcinoma (24% and 24%), p<0.001. Genotype separates them: a DAXX, ATRX or MEN1 mutation was present in 35 of 63 (57%) low and intermediate grade tumours and in 3 of 4 sequenced transformed tumours against 0 of 28 carcinomas; Rb protein was lost in 0% of well-differentiated tumours of any grade against 59% of carcinomas; and p53 immunoreactivity was abnormal in 0% against 56%.",
     "avoid": "Do not route a well-differentiated G3 tumour down a small-cell carcinoma pathway, and do not treat a poorly differentiated carcinoma as a NET because the Ki-67 happens to be 25%. NANETS reports a multi-institutional pathological review in which only 44 of 107 resected pancreatic tumours originally called poorly differentiated carcinoma actually were; that review is not in this page's full-text depot and the figure is quoted as NANETS states it.",
     "note": "Read the survival contrast carefully. In the stage-matched analysis restricted to stage IV, pancreatic grade 1-2 well-differentiated tumours and those with a high-grade component showed no statistically significant difference in disease-specific survival, and both did far better than poorly differentiated carcinoma (median 61 against 16 months, p<0.001; hazard ratios 0.17 and 0.16 against carcinoma as reference). The 55-against-162-month comparison is unmatched, and it is the one the abstract leads with. The 31 cases were assembled by searching two pathology archives for grade discrepancy, so the series cannot say how often this happens, the genotype contrast rests on four prospectively sequenced tumours against literature controls, and 6 of the 31 were biopsies only in which the coexisting lower-grade component was inferred from clinical history rather than seen. In challenging cases, particularly in the pancreas, NCCN lists Rb, p53, p16, ATRX and DAXX as an optional panel to help distinguish G3 NET from carcinoma, read together with the clinical, functional-imaging and molecular picture. See clinical decision 8 for what each diagnosis then means."
    },
    {
     "t": "Treat a grade obtained from a needle biopsy as a floor, not a fact — biopsy systematically understates grade in G2 disease.",
     "l": "Standard",
     "g": "C",
     "refs": [
      "24750272",
      "31856076"
     ],
     "pref": "Any observation-versus-resection decision that rests on grade. In 46 tumours sampled by EUS-FNA at one centre, 33 of which were resected and available for comparison, agreement between readers was excellent within each modality (Pearson r-squared 0.93 on cytology and 0.94 on the resection specimen, both p<0.001, with no grade disagreement between readers) - but agreement between cytological and histological grade was poor: kappa 0.21 (p=0.09), rising only to 0.24 (p=0.06) when restricted to the 27 cases with at least 200 cells counted, and no better at a 5% cut-off than at 2%. Cytology under-graded systematically: 10 of 14 histological G2 tumours (71%) were called cytological G1, and histological Ki-67 averaged 1.3 times the cytological value. Cytological grade still separated the worst group - actuarial progression-free survival 10 plus or minus 4 months for cytological G3 against 29 plus or minus 7 for G2 and 68 plus or minus 10 for G1 (p<0.0001) - but cytological G1 and G2 did not differ for progression-free or overall survival.",
     "avoid": "Do not promise a patient that a G1 biopsy means a G1 tumour. NANETS reports agreement of tumour grade between EUS-FNA cytology and the resection specimen in under 50% of G2 and G3 cases, and areas with Ki-67 of 2% or less were common even within G2 tumours. The only prospective study of fine-needle core biopsy in non-functional tumours found 83% concordance, in 30 patients; that study is quoted from the NANETS text and is not in this page's full-text depot.",
     "note": "Two cautions on the study itself. The four cytological G3 patients who drive the significant survival separation were all locally advanced, node-positive or metastatic at diagnosis, so cytological G3 may be marking stage rather than grade; and the concordance analysis could only include the resected tumours, so nothing in it describes how cytology performs in the small lesions actually being watched. Progression-free survival was also calculated independently of whether the tumour was removed, mixing resected and unresected patients in the same curves. Where additional tissue is needed for immunohistochemistry, add core biopsy to aspiration where it is available. [EXPERTISE]"
    }
   ],
   "alt": [
    {
     "t": "For a small incidental suspected nonfunctioning pNET, discuss whether tissue confirmation will change observation or treatment; ENETS recommends confirmation where possible.",
     "l": "Reasonable",
     "g": "D",
     "refs": [
      "31856076",
      "37877341",
      "35986682"
     ],
     "pref": "An asymptomatic sub-centimetre lesion with characteristic arterial enhancement where the plan is surveillance whatever the grade. NANETS states that in such patients biopsy is not routinely necessary to confirm the diagnosis before deciding to observe.",
     "avoid": "Do not skip tissue when the diagnosis is genuinely in question, when grade would change the plan, or when the lesion is 1-2 cm and the observe-or-resect decision is live - that is exactly the decision grade is meant to inform. And know that the guidelines disagree here. ENETS 2023, read in full, states that a suspected nonfunctioning tumour under 2 cm with positive somatostatin-receptor imaging should be confirmed histologically or cytologically where possible (level 3 evidence, grade B), and notes DAXX and ATRX loss and alternative lengthening of telomeres as independent adverse prognostic factors particularly in tumours of 2 cm or less. The 2025 MEN1 recommendations go the other way again and find no role for routine EUS-guided biopsy in that syndrome. See the limited-evidence section and approval 11.",
     "note": "The ASPEN study required a positive fine-needle aspirate or biopsy, or a positive 68Ga-labelled DOTA PET, before enrolment - but in practice 170 of its 500 patients (34%) never had an aspirate, it was negative in a further 45 (9%), and grade was not evaluable in 68 of the 285 who did have one (23.9%). So its reassuring surveillance figures come from a population in which the diagnosis was often established by receptor PET alone and in which the surveillance arm has no histological characterisation at all."
    },
    {
     "t": "Order molecular profiling where the disease is locoregionally unresectable or metastatic and the patient is a candidate for systemic therapy.",
     "l": "Reasonable",
     "g": "D",
     "refs": [
      "36924180"
     ],
     "pref": "Tumour tissue is preferred; circulating tumour DNA is an option when tissue testing is not feasible. ENETS encourages molecular profiling in neuroendocrine carcinoma specifically, to identify new targets, while saying plainly that the targets are not yet established.",
     "avoid": "Do not profile a small localised G1 tumour that is going to be observed or enucleated: nothing in the result changes that decision, and there is no established targeted therapy in this setting."
    }
   ],
   "avoid": [
    {
     "t": "Do not let a hormone immunostain decide whether the tumour is functional.",
     "l": "Avoid",
     "g": "D",
     "refs": [
      "37578384"
     ],
     "pref": "Functional status is a clinical syndrome plus biochemical evidence of inappropriately raised hormone — that is the ENETS definition and it is what clinical decision 3 works from.",
     "avoid": "NCCN states that hormone staining by immunohistochemistry is not helpful and that a positive stain does not mean there is a functional tumour. Chasing a positive insulin stain in an asymptomatic normoglycaemic patient produces an operation nobody needed."
    },
    {
     "t": "Do not accept the diagnostic label \"carcinoma with neuroendocrine features\".",
     "l": "Avoid",
     "g": "D",
     "pref": "Ask for a definite WHO classification. Where the histology is genuinely ambiguous the report should say so, recommend clinical correlation and recommend a broad next-generation sequencing panel.",
     "avoid": "Adenocarcinomas of the GI tract often express neuroendocrine markers patchily with no survival or management significance, and that patchy expression is a common route into the wrong pathway. In higher-grade pancreatic neoplasms, trypsin, chymotrypsin and BCL10 help exclude an acinar cell carcinoma expressing neuroendocrine markers."
    }
   ]
  },
  {
   "id": "2",
   "tone": "cure",
   "name": "2 · Stage the disease",
   "req": "all",
   "crit": [
    "Multiphasic CT or MRI of the abdomen, with arterial and portal venous phases, covering the whole pancreas",
    "Somatostatin-receptor PET/CT or PET/MRI where receptor status or occult metastatic disease would change the plan",
    "Chest CT, and FDG-PET where the tumour is G2 or higher",
    "Main pancreatic duct calibre, tumour calcification and cystic morphology recorded explicitly",
    "Liver and nodal status stated before any operation is booked"
   ],
   "ask": "What is the disease extent, and do functional imaging findings suggest tumor heterogeneity?",
   "standard": [
    {
     "t": "If staging shows hepatic metastases, the hepatic disease is the NELM pathway from here — this page covers the primary only.",
     "l": "Standard",
     "g": "D",
     "refs": [
      "31856076"
     ],
     "pref": "Hand off at this assessment, by name, as soon as liver deposits are seen. The NELM page carries hepatic tumour burden and distribution, cytoreduction thresholds, liver-directed modality choice, systemic sequencing for grade 1–2 and high-grade disease, carcinoid-crisis precautions and the transplant question. It also carries the decision about resecting the pancreatic primary when liver metastases are present, where NANETS reached no consensus and the majority view was that resection may help only in selected circumstances.",
     "avoid": "Do not make the primary-resection decision in metastatic disease on this page. Two specific warnings travel with the patient: NCCN states that pancreatoduodenectomy in metastatic disease is usually not curative and affects liver-directed therapy long term, and that liver-directed therapies for hepatic metastases after pancreatoduodenectomy carry an increased risk of cholangitis and liver abscess. That makes the sequence a joint decision between this assessment and the NELM pathway, not a pancreatic one.",
     "note": "Locoregionally advanced unresectable disease without liver metastases is also outside this page's scope: it is a systemic-therapy decision and NCCN's pancreatic NET systemic principles apply."
    },
    {
     "t": "Use somatostatin-receptor PET rather than octreotide scintigraphy, and read it together with multiphase contrast CT or MRI in the same sitting where the scanner allows it.",
     "l": "Standard",
     "g": "C",
     "refs": [
      "26712231",
      "36725249",
      "31856076"
     ],
     "pref": "Staging where occult metastatic disease would change the operation, and localising a primary in a patient who presents with metastases. In a prospective single-centre study of 131 patients imaged with all three modalities and read independently and blind, 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT detected 847 of 891 lesions, 95.1% (95% CI 92.4-96.8), against 404 of 891, 45.3% (37.9-52.9), for anatomic imaging and 275 of 891, 30.9% (25.0-37.5), for 111In-pentetreotide SPECT/CT (p<0.001 for both comparisons), and the PET changed the management recommendation in 43 of 131 patients (32.8%). A previously unknown primary was found in 4 of 14 patients (28.6%).",
     "avoid": "Do not read the PET alone. Contrast CT or MRI is what identifies the receptor-negative deposits, and NCCN requires the two together. Acceptable tracers are 68Ga-DOTATATE, 68Ga-DOTATOC and 64Cu-DOTATATE; a lesion counts as receptor-positive when uptake exceeds liver, and the modified Krenning score runs 0 none, 1 very low, 2 at or below liver, 3 above liver, 4 above spleen.",
     "note": "Grade C, downgraded on the full-text read, and the detection figures have to be read against their reference standard. The denominator of 891 lesions is the union of lesions seen on any of the three tests, which structurally pushes the most sensitive modality toward 100% and the others downward. In the 25 patients (19%) who were operated and so had histology, per-lesion true positives fell to 72 of 113 (63.7%) for the PET, 44 of 113 (38.9%) for CT or MRI and 25 of 113 (22.1%) for SPECT/CT - and all 38 histologically proven lesions missed by every imaging test were nodal metastases. Only 110 of the 891 lesions were pancreatic, the cohort was enriched for MEN1 and VHL by inclusion criterion, change in management was adjudicated unblinded by the team that ordered the scans, and there are no follow-up or outcome data. Receptor PET is not a surveillance test: NCCN states that somatostatin-receptor imaging and FDG-PET are not recommended for routine surveillance, and the SNMMI/EANM standard adds that a rise or fall in lesional uptake must not be read as response or progression the way it would be with other tracers. [EXPERTISE]"
    },
    {
     "t": "Record the main pancreatic duct calibre, any calcification and whether the lesion is cystic — all three carry information that size does not.",
     "l": "Standard",
     "g": "D",
     "refs": [
      "35986682",
      "36434481"
     ],
     "pref": "Every lesion being considered for observation. In 981 patients resected for well-differentiated tumours at eight centres, calcification was present in 122 of 697 assessable patients (18%) and a predominantly cystic appearance in 120 of 702 (17%).         "CLARINET establishes that lanreotide 120 mg delays radiographic progression in somatostatin-receptor-positive, grade 1 or 2 enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, with a hazard ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.30–0.73) and 65.1% versus 33.0% progression-free at 24 months, and it does so across hepatic tumour volumes above and below 25%.         "CLARINET’s grade 2 subgroup HR was 0.45 (95% CI 0.22–0.91). The HR 0.58 (0.32–1.04) belongs to the pancreatic-primary subgroup. Subgroup estimates do not establish differential benefit by grade or primary site.",

        "The whole benefit is radiographic.         "The size of the effect is unknown because the trial ended before it could be measured.         "Progression-free survival and time to tumour progression return the identical 18.0-month placebo median from different event counts (60 against 58), which shows the median sits in a sparse region of the curve where two events make no difference to the estimate.",
        "The chromogranin A result is reported on 64 of 101 and 64 of 103 patients, roughly two-thirds of each arm, with no account of the missing third, and it is a biochemical change in a non-functioning tumour population where it carries no symptomatic meaning.",

        "The trial excluded any prior radionuclide therapy at any time, chemoembolisation or chemotherapy within 6 months, and more than 15 days of previous somatostatin analogue.         "The discussion raises the obvious reading of its own data, that an 18-month placebo median supports watchful waiting, and sets it aside on the ground that the study examined prevention of progression.         "The adverse events that matter for a surgical population are presented as reassurance.         "The sponsor controlled the trial end to end.         "Do not make it mandatory for every patient.         "Neither trial established an overall-survival benefit — CLARINET found no significant difference in overall survival or quality of life, and PROMID is an interim analysis at 67 progressions and 16 deaths of a trial that enrolled 85 of a planned 162 patients and was then closed for slow accrual, so its confirmatory survival analysis at 121 deaths was never performed.         "Continue the somatostatin analogue for functional-syndrome control where it is needed, and after clinically significant progression in a nonfunctional tumour do not automatically continue it for antiproliferative benefit.",

        "FGFR2 fusion or rearrangement",
        "C",
        "Preferred for a defined phenotype. Pemigatinib after prior systemic therapy, or futibatinib after gemcitabine–platinum.         "Do not infer superiority over second-line chemotherapy: both trials are single-arm, neither has been compared with it, and The pemigatinib investigators explicitly warn against the cross-study comparison with pooled second-line chemotherapy (response 9.5%, progression-free survival 2.6 months) that makes the agent look better.
